triage.name: Diabetes Type 1
triage.reason: Classic presentation with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss and possible DKA; diagnosis reachable by history, labs and ketone assessment.

demographics: Slight male predominance in childhood-onset disease
More common in people of Northern European descent

risk_factors.text: Personal history of another autoimmune disease (thyroid, celiac, adrenal)

family_history: Type 1 diabetes in a parent or sibling

chief_complaints.text: I'm so thirsty all the time
I'm peeing all the time, even at night
I'm exhausted and can't keep up
I've been throwing up and my stomach hurts

hpi.onset: Abrupt, over days to a few weeks; often after a viral illness
hpi.duration: Days to weeks at presentation; DKA can bring patients in within 24–48 hours of worsening
hpi.progression: Rapidly worsening thirst, urination and fatigue; without insulin, progresses to vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing and confusion
hpi.location: Generalized; abdominal pain when present is diffuse or periumbilical
hpi.quality: Constant thirst and frequent urination; abdominal pain is dull and crampy
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; children may be lethargic or difficult to arouse if ketoacidosis is advanced
hpi.timing: Constant; urination continues through the night

associated_symptoms.text: Drinking large amounts of water and still feeling thirsty
Weight loss despite a good appetite
Tingling or numbness in the feet or hands
Sores that are slow to heal

pertinent_negatives: No fever with dysuria or flank pain
No polyuria from a diuretic or excessive water drinking alone
No gradual weight gain with dark velvety skin folds
No recent head trauma or seizure

positives.text: Bedwetting in a previously dry child
Tingling or numbness in the feet

atypical.how_it_differs: Toddlers and infants present with irritability, poor feeding, failure to thrive, heavy wet diapers and new bedwetting rather than clear thirst complaints.
missing_classic_features: Weight loss reported by the patient

atypical.how_it_differs: Onset can be slower and symptoms mistaken for normal aging; patients may present with dehydration, confusion or weight loss rather than classic thirst.
Type 1 can occur in people with obesity and be mistaken for type 2; they may still have ketosis-prone disease and need insulin.
May first appear or worsen during pregnancy with severe hyperglycemia, and can be confused with gestational diabetes.

general.mild: Alert, well-appearing but tired; may look thin
general.moderate: Lethargic, dry mucous membranes, appears dehydrated
general.severe: Ill-appearing, markedly dehydrated, deep sighing respirations, fruity breath
general.critical: Obtunded or unresponsive, severely dehydrated, Kussmaul breathing, shock

findings.maneuver: Observe body habitus and compare with prior weight if available
findings.finding: Recent unintentional weight loss; lean or wasted appearance

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral mucosa and tongue
findings.finding: Dry, tacky mucous membranes; sunken eyes

findings.maneuver: Observe the respiratory pattern and effort
findings.finding: Deep, rapid, sighing respirations without retractions

findings.maneuver: Palpate the radial pulse and auscultate the heart
Measure blood pressure with the patient seated or supine
findings.finding: Low blood pressure, worse on standing

findings.maneuver: Press the nail bed and release, timing refill

findings.finding: Diffuse or periumbilical tenderness without guarding or rebound

findings.maneuver: Check visual acuity and ask about blurring
findings.finding: Blurred vision that improves with glucose control

findings.maneuver: Test light touch and vibration sense in the feet
findings.finding: Decreased sensation in a stocking distribution
Clear breath sounds without crackles or wheeze

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin for rashes, ulcers or velvety patches
findings.finding: No rash, no acanthosis nigricans, no chronic ulcers
No focal deficit, normal mental status when not in DKA

labs.caveat: Fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher, or a random glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher with classic symptoms, supports the diagnosis. Values above 250 mg/dL raise concern for ketoacidosis.
A1c of 6.5% or higher meets a diagnostic threshold. It reflects average glucose over about 3 months and can be falsely low in rapid-onset disease, anemia, or hemoglobin variants.
Low bicarbonate reflects metabolic acidosis from ketoacidosis. A value below 18 mmol/L with ketones and hyperglycemia supports DKA.
Total body potassium is depleted even when serum potassium looks normal or high; insulin and fluid shifts can cause a dangerous drop. Potassium must be checked before and during insulin therapy.
Dilutional hyponatremia from hyperglycemia and fluid loss; corrected sodium is higher than measured. A high corrected sodium in DKA suggests severe free-water loss.
Rises with dehydration and prerenal azotemia; usually improves with fluids. Persistent elevation suggests acute kidney injury.
Elevated from dehydration and catabolism; the BUN/creatinine ratio is often high.
Low in DKA from osmotic diuresis and intracellular shift; severe hypophosphatemia can cause weakness and respiratory depression.
High in hyperglycemic dehydration; helps assess severity and guide fluid therapy.
Leukocytosis is common in DKA from stress and dehydration and does not by itself mean infection.
Glucose appears in urine once the blood level exceeds the renal threshold; a strong positive supports hyperglycemia.
Urine ketones confirm ketosis. The nitroprusside method mainly detects acetoacetate and can underestimate ketones early in DKA; serum beta-hydroxybutyrate is more accurate when available.
Screen for autoimmune thyroid disease, which clusters with type 1 diabetes.
Order with TSH if thyroid disease is suspected.
Check only if Addison disease is suspected (unexplained hypotension, hyperkalemia, or hyponatremia that does not fit DKA).

findings.finding: Prolonged QT from hypokalemia or hypocalcemia
ST depression or nonspecific ST-T changes from electrolyte disturbance

findings.text: Usually normal; no infiltrate, effusion, or pneumothorax
Findings of infection or aspiration if present

initial.why: Confirms hyperglycemia; a random level of 200 mg/dL or higher with classic symptoms is diagnostic
Assesses bicarbonate, potassium, sodium, and kidney function; low bicarbonate suggests ketoacidosis
Urine glucose and ketones support the diagnosis and assess ketosis
Confirms chronic hyperglycemia and meets a diagnostic threshold at 6.5% or higher
Baseline white count and blood counts; leukocytosis is common in DKA
Phosphate is often low in DKA and can fall further with insulin
Looks for infection or other cause of acidosis
initial.only_if: infection is suspected (fever, cough, hypoxia, or abnormal lung exam)

confirmatory.why: Directly confirms ketosis and is more accurate than urine ketones in early DKA
Confirms autoimmune beta-cell destruction and distinguishes type 1 from type 2 or monogenic diabetes
Low or undetectable levels confirm insulin deficiency

supporting.why: Screens for associated autoimmune thyroid disease
Confirms thyroid status if TSH is abnormal
Evaluates for Addison disease when hypotension, hyperkalemia, or hyponatremia is unexplained

not_indicated.why: Not routine in an otherwise well patient without respiratory symptoms or signs of infection
No role in the diagnosis of type 1 diabetes
No role in the diagnosis of type 1 diabetes
Not needed unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis

decision_points: Check potassium before giving insulin; insulin drives potassium into cells and can cause dangerous hypokalemia
If DKA is present, treat as a medical emergency with fluids, insulin, and electrolyte replacement
Distinguish type 1 from type 2 when the presentation is atypical (older age, obesity, or no ketosis) using autoantibodies and C-peptide
Screen for associated autoimmune conditions such as thyroid disease and celiac disease

criteria.name: Diagnostic thresholds for diabetes
criteria.summary: Diabetes is diagnosed by a fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher, a 2-hour glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher during an oral glucose tolerance test, an A1c of 6.5% or higher, or a random glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher with classic symptoms. Abnormal results are usually confirmed with a repeat test unless symptoms are clear.
items: 2-hour glucose 200 mg/dL or higher on oral glucose tolerance test
Random glucose 200 mg/dL or higher with classic symptoms

criteria.name: Diabetic ketoacidosis criteria
criteria.summary: DKA is suggested by hyperglycemia (often above 250 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis with low bicarbonate, and ketonemia or ketonuria. It is a life-threatening emergency requiring fluids, insulin, and electrolyte replacement.
items: Bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L and pH below 7.30

differential.name: Diabetic ketoacidosis
differential.why_considered: Type 1 diabetes commonly presents in or progresses to ketoacidosis, with vomiting, abdominal pain, and deep breathing that can be mistaken for the primary diagnosis itself.
differential.trigger: Vomiting, abdominal pain, deep rapid breathing, or fruity breath in a patient with hyperglycemia

history: Rapid worsening over hours to a day or two
Marked thirst and urination with weight loss
labs: Bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L with pH below 7.30

differential.name: Type 2 diabetes
differential.why_considered: The most common cause of hyperglycemia; can present with thirst, urination, and weight loss, especially in older or overweight patients.

history: Gradual onset over months to years
Often overweight or obese with acanthosis nigricans
exam: No Kussmaul breathing or acetone breath

differential.name: Diabetes insipidus
differential.why_considered: Causes severe polyuria and polydipsia, mimicking the classic presentation of type 1 diabetes.

history: Large volumes of dilute urine, often with a preference for ice water
May follow head trauma, neurosurgery, or lithium use
exam: Signs of dehydration if water access is limited
labs: Normal or near-normal glucose and A1c
Low urine osmolality with high serum osmolality

differential.name: Urinary tract infection
differential.why_considered: Frequent urination, abdominal discomfort, and sometimes nausea can be attributed to a urinary infection, especially in children.

labs: Positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites on urinalysis

differential.name: Viral gastroenteritis
differential.why_considered: Vomiting, abdominal pain, and dehydration can resemble early DKA, particularly in children.

history: Diarrhea and vomiting in a patient with sick contacts
No chronic thirst or weight loss
exam: Signs of dehydration but no Kussmaul breathing

differential.name: Addison disease
differential.why_considered: Autoimmune adrenal insufficiency clusters with type 1 diabetes and can cause fatigue, weight loss, nausea, and hypotension.
differential.trigger: Unexplained hypotension, hyperkalemia, or hyponatremia that does not fit DKA

history: Chronic fatigue, weakness, and weight loss
Salt craving and dizziness on standing
Hyperpigmentation of skin creases and mucosa
labs: Low morning cortisol with elevated ACTH

severity.mild: Early, uncomplicated: mild polyuria and polydipsia, no dehydration, glucose 126–200 mg/dL, no ketosis
severity.moderate: Established hyperglycemia with dehydration and fatigue, glucose 200–350 mg/dL, trace to small ketones, bicarbonate 15–20 mmol/L
severity.severe: Ketoacidosis: vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing, glucose 350–600 mg/dL, moderate to large ketones, bicarbonate 8–15 mmol/L
severity.critical: Severe DKA or hyperglycemic crisis: obtundation, shock, glucose above 500 mg/dL, bicarbonate below 8 mmol/L, pH below 7.1, or significant electrolyte disturbance

red_flags.meaning: Severe metabolic acidosis from ketoacidosis; needs immediate fluids and insulin
Significant ketone production; DKA until proven otherwise
May signal DKA rather than a surgical abdomen; check glucose and ketones
Severe dehydration, acidosis, or cerebral edema; emergency
Volume depletion or shock; requires urgent fluid resuscitation

red_flags.finding: Potassium below 3.3 mmol/L or above 5.5 mmol/L
red_flags.meaning: Dangerous electrolyte disturbance; insulin can worsen hypokalemia

complications.name: Cerebral edema
clues: Headache and vomiting during DKA treatment

complications.name: Diabetic retinopathy
clues: Microaneurysms and hemorrhages on dilated eye exam

complications.name: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy
clues: Numbness and tingling in a stocking distribution
Reduced vibration and light touch sensation

special_populations.differences: Younger children present with irritability, poor feeding, heavy wet diapers, and new bedwetting; DKA is more common at diagnosis and cerebral edema is a feared complication during treatment.

Onset can be slower and symptoms mistaken for aging; they may present with dehydration, confusion, or weight loss rather than classic thirst, and have higher rates of cardiovascular and renal complications.
May first appear or worsen during pregnancy with severe hyperglycemia and can be confused with gestational diabetes; tight glucose control is critical to reduce fetal risks.
Type 1 can occur in people with obesity and be mistaken for type 2; they may still have ketosis-prone disease and require insulin.

key_questions.question: How much have you been drinking and urinating, and has it changed recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Marked polydipsia and polyuria, including waking at night to urinate or new bedwetting in a previously dry child

key_questions.question: When did these symptoms start, and how quickly have they gotten worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Abrupt onset over days to a few weeks, often after a viral illness, with rapid progression

key_questions.question: Have you lost weight without trying?
key_questions.looking_for: Unintentional weight loss despite a good appetite, supporting insulin deficiency

key_questions.question: Have you had nausea, vomiting, or belly pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Vomiting and diffuse or periumbilical abdominal pain suggesting ketoacidosis rather than a surgical abdomen

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any changes in your breathing, or does your breath smell fruity?
key_questions.looking_for: Deep, rapid breathing (Kussmaul) or acetone breath indicating severe ketoacidosis

key_questions.question: Have you felt more tired, sleepy, or confused than usual?
key_questions.looking_for: Lethargy or altered mental status suggesting severe dehydration, acidosis, or cerebral edema

key_questions.question: Has your vision been blurry?
key_questions.looking_for: Blurred vision that improves with glucose control, from osmotic lens changes

key_questions.question: Have you had any tingling, numbness, or sores that are slow to heal?
key_questions.looking_for: Peripheral neuropathy or poor wound healing, more typical of long-standing disease

key_questions.question: Do you have any other medical conditions, especially thyroid disease, celiac disease, or adrenal problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Other autoimmune diseases that cluster with type 1 diabetes

key_questions.question: Are you taking any medications, including steroids or diuretics?
key_questions.looking_for: Steroids or diuretics that can raise glucose or cause polyuria and mimic the presentation

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have type 1 diabetes, thyroid disease, or celiac disease?
key_questions.looking_for: First-degree relative with type 1 diabetes or another autoimmune condition

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent infections or illnesses?
key_questions.looking_for: A recent viral illness that may have triggered the onset

reasoning_points: Abrupt onset over days to weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, and unintentional weight loss in a child, adolescent, or young adult
Hyperglycemia confirmed by a random glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher with classic symptoms, a fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher, or an A1c of 6.5% or higher
Ketosis or ketoacidosis suggested by vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath, low bicarbonate, and positive serum or urine ketones
Insulin deficiency confirmed by low or undetectable C-peptide and positive islet autoantibodies such as GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8, or insulin
Absence of features of type 2 diabetes such as gradual onset, central obesity, acanthosis nigricans, and preserved C-peptide
Other causes of polyuria and polydipsia excluded, including diabetes insipidus, urinary tract infection, and viral gastroenteritis
Associated autoimmune conditions considered, including thyroid disease, celiac disease, and Addison disease

easy: Child or adolescent with classic polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss
Random glucose above 200 mg/dL with classic symptoms
Positive urine ketones and low bicarbonate
medium: Presents with vomiting and abdominal pain that is mistaken for gastroenteritis or a surgical abdomen
Older adult with slower onset and symptoms attributed to aging
Patient with obesity where type 2 diabetes is initially assumed
Mild hyperglycemia without obvious ketosis at presentation
hard: Toddler with irritability, poor feeding, heavy wet diapers, and new bedwetting rather than clear thirst complaints
Pregnant patient with severe hyperglycemia mistaken for gestational diabetes
DKA with normal or high serum potassium masking total body potassium depletion
Concurrent autoimmune disease such as Addison disease altering the presentation
Atypical diabetes with features of both type 1 and type 2 requiring autoantibodies and C-peptide to classify
